claim: Gzma-/- mice have a mixed C57BL/6J and C57BL/6N genetic background.
source: We show herein that Gzma-/- mice have a mixed C57BL/6J and C57BL/6N genetic background and retain the full-length nicotinamide nucleotide transhydrogenase (Nnt) gene, whereas Nnt is truncated in C57BL/6J mice.
evidence: Supported by whole-genome sequencing data showing approximately 60% of the genome has C57BL/6N SNPs and indels, with the rest reflecting a 6J background (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

claim: Gzma-/- mice retain the full-length nicotinamide nucleotide transhydrogenase (Nnt) gene.
source: We show herein that Gzma-/- mice have a mixed C57BL/6J and C57BL/6N genetic background and retain the full-length nicotinamide nucleotide transhydrogenase (Nnt) gene, whereas Nnt is truncated in C57BL/6J mice.
evidence: Demonstrated by WGS alignment to C3H/HeJ genome (Figure 3c), RNA-Seq Sashimi plots (Figure 3d), and RT-PCR showing longer PCR product (Figure 3e).

claim: Nnt is truncated in C57BL/6J mice.
source: We show herein that Gzma-/- mice have a mixed C57BL/6J and C57BL/6N genetic background and retain the full-length nicotinamide nucleotide transhydrogenase (Nnt) gene, whereas Nnt is truncated in C57BL/6J mice.
evidence: Supported by previous literature citations (Freeman et al., 2006; Fontaine and Davis, 2016) and confirmed by WGS and RNA-Seq data in this study.

claim: Chikungunya viral arthritis was substantially ameliorated in Gzma-/- mice.
source: Chikungunya viral arthritis was substantially ameliorated in Gzma-/- mice; however, the presence of Nnt and the C57BL/6N background, rather than loss of GZMA expression, was responsible for this phenotype.
evidence: Shown by foot swelling measurements in Figure 1a where Gzma-/- mice showed significantly reduced foot swelling compared to 6J mice from day 3 to day 10 (p<0.002).

claim: The presence of Nnt and the C57BL/6N background, rather than loss of GZMA expression, was responsible for ameliorated CHIKV arthritis in Gzma-/- mice.
source: Chikungunya viral arthritis was substantially ameliorated in Gzma-/- mice; however, the presence of Nnt and the C57BL/6N background, rather than loss of GZMA expression, was responsible for this phenotype.
evidence: Demonstrated by experiments showing 6N mice (with intact Nnt) also showed reduced foot swelling (Figure 1a), and 6N∆Nnt8-12 mice (with Nnt deletion) showed increased foot swelling comparable to 6J mice (Figure 4a).

claim: GzmaS211A mice are a new CRISPR active site mutant C57BL/6J mouse.
source: A new CRISPR active site mutant C57BL/6J GzmaS211A mouse provided the first insights into GZMA's bioactivity free of background issues, with circulating proteolytically active GZMA promoting immune-stimulating and pro-inflammatory signatures.
evidence: Generated using CRISPR technology with the reactive site serine changed to alanine (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a–c), with loss of enzyme activity confirmed by BLT assays (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d).

claim: Circulating proteolytically active GZMA promotes immune-stimulating and pro-inflammatory signatures.
source: A new CRISPR active site mutant C57BL/6J GzmaS211A mouse provided the first insights into GZMA's bioactivity free of background issues, with circulating proteolytically active GZMA promoting immune-stimulating and pro-inflammatory signatures.
evidence: Demonstrated by RNA-Seq analysis of GzmaS211A vs 6J mice after poly(I:C) injection showing downregulation of inflammation and leukocyte activation signatures in GzmaS211A mice (Figure 6b, Supplementary file 6f).

claim: Approximately 27% of Run Accessions listing C57BL/6J as the mouse strain had Nnt sequencing reads inconsistent with a C57BL/6J genetic background.
source: Remarkably, k-mer mining of the Sequence Read Archive illustrated that ≈27% of Run Accessions and ≈38% of BioProjects listing C57BL/6J as the mouse strain had Nnt sequencing reads inconsistent with a C57BL/6J genetic background.
evidence: k-mer mining analysis revealed that 1008 of 3744 Run Accessions (≈27%) had reads aligning to both Nnt exons 2 and 9, indicating full-length Nnt inconsistent with 6J background (Supplementary file 7a).

claim: Approximately 38% of BioProjects listing C57BL/6J as the mouse strain had Nnt sequencing reads inconsistent with a C57BL/6J genetic background.
source: Remarkably, k-mer mining of the Sequence Read Archive illustrated that ≈27% of Run Accessions and ≈38% of BioProjects listing C57BL/6J as the mouse strain had Nnt sequencing reads inconsistent with a C57BL/6J genetic background.
evidence: 38% (15% plus 23%) of BioProjects had Run Accessions with 'C57BL/6J' strain listings not compatible with a 6J background based on k-mer mining analysis.

claim: GZMA is a serine protease secreted by cytotoxic lymphocytes.
source: Granzyme A (GZMA) is a granule trypsin-like serine protease (trypase) secreted by cytotoxic lymphocytes such as NK cells (Fehniger et al., 2007; Wu et al., 2019), NKT cells (Gordy et al., 2011), and CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes (Suhrbier et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by multiple literature citations describing GZMA as a serine protease secreted by various cytotoxic lymphocyte populations.

claim: GZMA is secreted by NK cells.
source: Granzyme A (GZMA) is a granule trypsin-like serine protease (trypase) secreted by cytotoxic lymphocytes such as NK cells (Fehniger et al., 2007; Wu et al., 2019), NKT cells (Gordy et al., 2011), and CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes (Suhrbier et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by citations (Fehniger et al., 2007; Wu et al., 2019) and confirmed by experiments showing NK cells as the likely source of GZMA after poly(I:C) treatment.

claim: GZMA is secreted by NKT cells.
source: Granzyme A (GZMA) is a granule trypsin-like serine protease (trypase) secreted by cytotoxic lymphocytes such as NK cells (Fehniger et al., 2007; Wu et al., 2019), NKT cells (Gordy et al., 2011), and CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes (Suhrbier et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by citation (Gordy et al., 2011).

claim: GZMA is secreted by CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes.
source: Granzyme A (GZMA) is a granule trypsin-like serine protease (trypase) secreted by cytotoxic lymphocytes such as NK cells (Fehniger et al., 2007; Wu et al., 2019), NKT cells (Gordy et al., 2011), and CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes (Suhrbier et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by citation (Suhrbier et al., 1991).

claim: Gzma-/- mice were generated using BL/6-III ES cells.
source: The strain origin of the BL/6-III ES cells used to generate Gzma-/- mice was only reported as C57BL/6 (Ebnet et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citation (Ebnet et al., 1995).

claim: BL/6-III ES cells have a C57BL/6N background.
source: As ES cells from 6J mice have a low rate of germline transmission, ES from 6N mice cells were frequently used to generate knockout mice (Fontaine and Davis, 2016), with our studies clearly arguing that BL/6-III ES cells also have a 6N background.
evidence: Inferred from WGS data showing Gzma-/- mice have a mixed 6N/6J background and full-length Nnt, combined with knowledge that ES cells from 6N mice were frequently used for knockout generation.

claim: C57BL/6J mice have a 5 exon deletion in the Nnt gene.
source: 6N mice have a full-length Nnt gene with 21 protein-coding exons, whereas 6J mice have an in-frame 5-exon deletion removing exons 7–11 (Freeman et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation (Freeman et al., 2006) and confirmed by WGS and RNA-Seq data in this study.

claim: C57BL/6J mice have lost exons 8–12 of 22 exons in the Nnt gene according to MM10 numbering.
source: Confusingly, the MM10 mouse build numbers the Nnt exons differently and includes the noncoding exon 1 that is located before the ATG start site. According to this numbering (which is used herein), 6J mice have lost exons 8–12 of 22 exons.
evidence: Explained by the authors based on the MM10 genome build annotation system.

claim: The Nnt gene is located approximately 6.2 megabases from the Gzma gene on mouse chromosome 13.
source: The Nnt gene is located only ≈6.2 megabases from the Gzma gene on mouse chromosome 13, so >30 backcrosses would be required to segregate these two loci (Silver, 2008; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and supported by citation (Silver, 2008).

claim: More than 30 backcrosses would be required to segregate the Nnt and Gzma loci.
source: The Nnt gene is located only ≈6.2 megabases from the Gzma gene on mouse chromosome 13, so >30 backcrosses would be required to segregate these two loci (Silver, 2008; Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Based on genetic distance calculations (Silver, 2008) and illustrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: NNT is located in the inner mitochondrial membrane.
source: The enzyme, nicotinamide nucleotide transhydrogenase (NNT), also known as proton-translocating NAD(P)+ transhydrogenase (EC 7.1.1.1), is located in the inner mitochondrial membrane and catalyzes the conversion of NADH plus NADP+ to NAD+ plus NADPH, while H+ is pumped from the inter-membrane space into the mitochondrial matrix (Rydström, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation (Rydström, 2006) and established scientific knowledge.

claim: NNT catalyzes the conversion of NADH plus NADP+ to NAD+ plus NADPH.
source: The enzyme, nicotinamide nucleotide transhydrogenase (NNT), also known as proton-translocating NAD(P)+ transhydrogenase (EC 7.1.1.1), is located in the inner mitochondrial membrane and catalyzes the conversion of NADH plus NADP+ to NAD+ plus NADPH, while H+ is pumped from the inter-membrane space into the mitochondrial matrix (Rydström, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation (Rydström, 2006) and established biochemical knowledge.

claim: NNT sustains mitochondrial antioxidant capacity through generation of NADPH.
source: NNT thereby sustains mitochondrial antioxidant capacity through generation of NADPH (Ward et al., 2020), with the loss of active NNT in 6J mice associated with reduced ability to detoxify reactive oxygen species (ROS) via the glutathione and thioredoxin pathways (McCambridge et al., 2019; Meimaridou et al., 2018; Ronchi et al., 2013; Rydström, 2006).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations (Ward et al., 2020; McCambridge et al., 2019; Meimaridou et al., 2018; Ronchi et al., 2013; Rydström, 2006).

claim: Loss of active NNT in 6J mice is associated with reduced ability to detoxify reactive oxygen species via the glutathione and thioredoxin pathways.
source: NNT thereby sustains mitochondrial antioxidant capacity through generation of NADPH (Ward et al., 2020), with the loss of active NNT in 6J mice associated with reduced ability to detoxify reactive oxygen species (ROS) via the glutathione and thioredoxin pathways (McCambridge et al., 2019; Meimaridou et al., 2018; Ronchi et al., 2013; Rydström, 2006).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations (McCambridge et al., 2019; Meimaridou et al., 2018; Ronchi et al., 2013; Rydström, 2006).

claim: GzmaS211A mice showed no significant differences in CHIKV arthritic foot swelling when compared with 6J mice.
source: However, we show herein that active site mutant GzmaS211A mice generated by CRISPR on a 6J background showed no significant differences in CHIKV arthritic foot swelling when compared with 6J mice.
evidence: Shown in Figure 1a where foot swelling was not significantly different between GzmaS211A and 6J mice.

claim: 6N mice showed a significant reduction in CHIKV-induced foot swelling when compared with 6J mice.
source: To test this contention, 6J and 6N mice (both Gzma+/+) were infected with CHIKV. 6N mice showed a significant reduction in foot swelling when compared with 6J mice (Figure 1a), arguing that the 6N background, rather than loss of GZMA expression, was primarily responsible for amelioration of foot swelling in Gzma-/- mice.
evidence: Shown in Figure 1a with statistical significance from day 3 to day 10.

claim: There were no significant differences in viremia for 6N, 6J, Gzma-/-, or GzmaS211A mice after CHIKV infection.
source: The reduced foot swelling in 6N and Gzma-/-mice was unlikely to be due to reduced viral loads as there were no significant differences in viremia for 6N, 6J, Gzma-/-, or GzmaS211A mice (Figure 1b).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1b.

claim: RNA-Seq of CHIKV-infected feet showed 1073 differentially expressed genes between Gzma-/- and 6J mice.
source: To gain insights into the reduced foot swelling in Gzma-/- mice (Figure 1a), RNA-Seq was undertaken on day 6 (peak arthritis) to compare gene expression in feet from CHIKV-infected Gzma-/- mice vs. 6J mice (NCBI BioProject PRJNA664644; full gene list in Supplementary file 2a). Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) (n = 1073) were generated after application of a q < 0.01 filter (Supplementary file 2b).
evidence: RNA-Seq data analysis with q < 0.01 filter applied (Supplementary file 2b).

claim: The dominant annotations for DEGs in Gzma-/- vs 6J CHIKV-infected feet were associated with decreased cell movement.
source: When the 1073 DEGs (for Gzma-/- + CHIKV vs. 6J + CHIKV; Supplementary file 2b) were analyzed for Diseases and Functions using Ingenuity Pathway Analysis (IPA), the dominant annotations were associated with decreased cell movement (often leukocyte migration) (Figure 2a, Supplementary file 2c).
evidence: IPA analysis shown in Figure 2a and Supplementary file 2c.

claim: A series of pro-inflammatory cytokine upstream regulators were downregulated in CHIKV-infected feet of Gzma-/- mice compared with 6J mice.
source: IPA upstream regulator (USR) analysis of the 1073 DEGs (Supplementary file 2d) also illustrated that a series of pro-inflammatory cytokine USRs were downregulated in the infected feet of Gzma-/- + CHIKV vs. 6J + CHIKV mice (Figure 2b, Supplementary file 2e), consistent with the reduced foot swelling seen in infected Gzma-/- mice when compared with infected 6J mice (Wilson et al., 2017).
evidence: IPA USR analysis shown in Figure 2b and Supplementary file 2e.

claim: Immunohistochemistry showed significantly reduced T cell and NK cells in arthritic infiltrates in feet after CHIKV infection of Gzma-/- mice compared with 6J mice.
source: These findings are consistent with immunohistochemistry data showing significantly reduced T cell and NK cells in the arthritic infiltrates in feet after CHIKV infection of Gzma-/- mice when compared with infected 6J mice (Wilson et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation (Wilson et al., 2017).

claim: Injection of proteolytically active recombinant mouse GZMA induced inflammatory foot swelling.
source: Injection of proteolytically active, but not proteolytically inactive, recombinant mouse GZMA induced inflammatory foot swelling, illustrating directly that GZMA's protease activity is able to drive pro-inflammatory responses (Schanoski et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation (Schanoski et al., 2019).

claim: Injection of proteolytically inactive recombinant mouse GZMA did not induce inflammatory foot swelling.
source: Injection of proteolytically active, but not proteolytically inactive, recombinant mouse GZMA induced inflammatory foot swelling, illustrating directly that GZMA's protease activity is able to drive pro-inflammatory responses (Schanoski et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation (Schanoski et al., 2019).

claim: GZMA expression in resting splenic NK cells was comparable for GzmaS211A and 6J mice.
source: Intracellular staining (Schanoski et al., 2019) showed that expression of the GZMA proteins in resting splenic NK cells (Fehniger et al., 2007) was comparable for GzmaS211A and 6J mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: Shown by FACS analysis in Figure 1—figure supplement 1e.

claim: Viral titers in feet were not significantly different for GzmaS211A and 6J mice after CHIKV infection.
source: When infected with CHIKV, viral titers in feet were not significantly different for GzmaS211A and 6J mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1f), arguing that enzymically active GZMA has no significant antiviral activity against CHIKV.
evidence: Shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1f.

claim: Enzymically active GZMA has no significant antiviral activity against CHIKV.
source: When infected with CHIKV, viral titers in feet were not significantly different for GzmaS211A and 6J mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1f), arguing that enzymically active GZMA has no significant antiviral activity against CHIKV.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of difference in viral titers between GzmaS211A and 6J mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1f).

claim: GZMA has no important antiviral function against CHIKV.
source: This is consistent with our previous study using Gzma-/- mice that also concluded that GZMA has no important antiviral function (Wilson et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation (Wilson et al., 2017) and current data from GzmaS211A mice.

claim: Serpinb6b effectively ameliorated CHIKV arthritic foot swelling in 6J mice.
source: The effective amelioration of CHIKV arthritic foot swelling in 6J mice following treatment with Serpinb6b (an inhibitor of GZMA) also supported the view that GZMA promotes inflammation in this setting (Wilson et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation (Wilson et al., 2017).

claim: Serpinb6b inhibited CHIKV foot swelling in GzmaS211A mice.
source: However, Serpinb6b also inhibited CHIKV foot swelling in GzmaS211A mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1g), arguing that Serpinb6b can inhibit other unknown proteases involved in promoting arthritic inflammation.
evidence: Shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1g.

claim: Serpinb6b can inhibit other unknown proteases involved in promoting arthritic inflammation.
source: However, Serpinb6b also inhibited CHIKV foot swelling in GzmaS211A mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1g), arguing that Serpinb6b can inhibit other unknown proteases involved in promoting arthritic inflammation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Serpinb6b inhibits foot swelling in GzmaS211A mice where GZMA is enzymatically inactive.

claim: The human orthologue of Serpinb6b, SerpinB6, has broad inhibitory activity.
source: The contention is supported by the broad inhibitory activity of the human orthologue, SerpinB6 (Strik et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation (Strik et al., 2004).

claim: Whole-genome sequencing demonstrated that Gzma-/- mice have approximately 60% of the genome showing SNPs and indels present in the C57BL/6N genome.
source: This analysis unequivocally demonstrated that Gzma-/- mice have a mixed genetic background, with ≈60% of the genome showing single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and indels present in the C57BL/6N (6N) genome (Mekada et al., 2015; Simon, 2013), with the rest reflecting a 6J background (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: WGS data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and supported by citations (Mekada et al., 2015; Simon, 2013).

claim: ES cells from 6J mice have a low rate of germline transmission.
source: As ES cells from 6J mice have a low rate of germline transmission, ES from 6N mice cells were frequently used to generate knockout mice (Fontaine and Davis, 2016), with our studies clearly arguing that BL/6-III ES cells also have a 6N background.
evidence: Supported by citation (Fontaine and Davis, 2016).

claim: ES cells from 6N mice were frequently used to generate knockout mice.
source: As ES cells from 6J mice have a low rate of germline transmission, ES from 6N mice cells were frequently used to generate knockout mice (Fontaine and Davis, 2016), with our studies clearly arguing that BL/6-III ES cells also have a 6N background.
evidence: Supported by citation (Fontaine and Davis, 2016).

claim: A large body of literature has resulted from the use of inbred Gzma-/- mice with 6J mice used as controls without being aware of the 6N background.
source: Importantly, a large body of literature has resulted from the use of inbred Gzma-/- mice (and Gzma-/-/Gzmb-/- double knockout mice derived from them) with 6J mice used as controls, without being aware of the presence and potential confounding influence of the 6N background (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Documented in Supplementary file 1 listing studies using Gzma-/- mice.

claim: 6N∆Nnt8-12 mice have the same deletion of Nnt exons as 6J mice.
source: To determine whether the Nnt gene deletion seen in 6J mice might be responsible for promoting the arthritic foot swelling in CHIKV-infected mice, we generated 6N∆Nnt8-12 mice wherein exons 8–12 of Nnt were deleted from 6N mice using CRISPR (Figure 4—figure supplement 1). 6N∆Nnt8-12 mice thus have the same deletion of Nnt exons as 6J mice.
evidence: Generated by CRISPR as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Foot swelling in 6N∆Nnt8-12 mice was significantly higher than in 6N mice after CHIKV infection.
source: Importantly, foot swelling in 6N∆Nnt8-12 mice was significantly higher than in 6N mice, with the Nnt exon 8–12 deletion increasing foot swelling to levels comparable to those seen in 6J mice (Figure 4a).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4a with statistical significance on days 2–7 (p values ranging from 0.0005 to 0.042).

claim: The Nnt exon 8–12 deletion increased foot swelling to levels comparable to those seen in 6J mice.
source: Importantly, foot swelling in 6N∆Nnt8-12 mice was significantly higher than in 6N mice, with the Nnt exon 8–12 deletion increasing foot swelling to levels comparable to those seen in 6J mice (Figure 4a).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4a.

claim: The absence of a functional Nnt gene can by itself promote overt foot swelling after CHIKV infection.
source: This data illustrates that the absence of a functional Nnt gene (6N∆Nnt8-12) can by itself promote overt foot swelling after CHIKV infection.
evidence: Demonstrated by the increased foot swelling in 6N∆Nnt8-12 mice compared to 6N mice (Figure 4a).

claim: The presence of functional Nnt gene in Gzma-/- mice likely contributes to the ameliorated foot swelling.
source: The data also argues that the presence of functional Nnt gene in Gzma-/- mice likely contributes to the ameliorated foot swelling seen in Gzma-/- mice.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that deletion of Nnt increases foot swelling, suggesting intact Nnt reduces foot swelling.

claim: The increased foot swelling in 6N∆Nnt8-12 mice was due primarily to increased edema.
source: Histology and H&E staining of arthritic feet illustrated that the increased foot swelling seen in 6N∆Nnt8-12 mice (compared with 6N mice) was due primarily to increased edema (Figure 4c and d), with no significant differences in cellular infiltrates (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a and b).
evidence: Shown by H&E staining in Figure 4c and quantitation in Figure 4d (p=0.005).

claim: There were no significant differences in cellular infiltrates between 6N∆Nnt8-12 and 6N mice after CHIKV infection.
source: Histology and H&E staining of arthritic feet illustrated that the increased foot swelling seen in 6N∆Nnt8-12 mice (compared with 6N mice) was due primarily to increased edema (Figure 4c and d), with no significant differences in cellular infiltrates (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a and b).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2a and b.

claim: Edema is a recognized feature of alphaviral arthritides.
source: Edema is a recognized feature of alphaviral arthritides and is well described in CHIKV mouse models (Gardner et al., 2010; Poo et al., 2014; Prow et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations (Gardner et al., 2010; Poo et al., 2014; Prow et al., 2019).

claim: There were no significant differences in T cell numbers in the inflammatory infiltrates between 6N∆Nnt8-12 and 6N mice.
source: Immunohistochemistry with anti-CD3 also showed no significant differences in T cell numbers in the inflammatory infiltrates (Figure 4—figure supplement 2c and d).
evidence: Shown by anti-CD3 immunohistochemistry in Figure 4—figure supplement 2c and d.

claim: MitoTEMPO treatment significantly ameliorated peak foot swelling in CHIKV-infected 6J mice.
source: Treatment of CHIKV arthritis in 6J mice with MitoTEMPO from day 3 to 8 post infection significantly ameliorated peak foot swelling (Figure 5a).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5a with statistical significance on days 6, 7, and 8 (p < 0.001).

claim: Viremia was not significantly affected by MitoTEMPO treatment.
source: Viremia was not significantly affected by MitoTEMPO treatment, even when treatment was initiated on day 0 (Figure 5b).
evidence: Shown in Figure 5b.

claim: MitoTEMPO treatment significantly reduced the cellular infiltrate in feet day 6 post CHIKV infection of 6J mice.
source: Histology and H&E staining revealed that MitoTEMPO treatment significantly reduced the cellular infiltrate in feet day 6 post CHIKV infection of 6J mice when compared with PBS treatment (Figure 5c and d).
evidence: Shown by H&E staining in Figure 5c and quantitation in Figure 5d (p=0.004).

claim: Edema was significantly reduced by MitoTEMPO treatment in CHIKV-infected 6J mice.
source: Edema was also significantly reduced by MitoTEMPO treatment (Figure 5e and f); additional images are shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.
evidence: Shown in Figure 5e and f (p=0.008).

claim: MitoTEMPO treatment and an intact Nnt gene in 6N mice provided overlapping anti-inflammatory activities.
source: MitoTEMPO treatment in 6J mice and an intact Nnt gene in 6N mice thus provided overlapping anti-inflammatory activities.
evidence: Demonstrated by IPA USR analysis showing 10 cytokine USRs downregulated in both comparisons (Figure 4e).

claim: Poly(I:C) injection i.v. into 6J mice resulted in mean peak serum GZMA levels of approximately 20 ng/ml after 2 hours.
source: We thus injected poly(I:C) i.v. into 6J mice and showed that serum GZMA levels reached mean peak serum levels of ≈20 ng/ml of serum after 2 hr, with levels dropping to baseline after 24 hr (Figure 6a).
evidence: Shown in Figure 6a.

claim: Serum GZMA levels dropped to baseline after 24 hours following poly(I:C) injection.
source: We thus injected poly(I:C) i.v. into 6J mice and showed that serum GZMA levels reached mean peak serum levels of ≈20 ng/ml of serum after 2 hr, with levels dropping to baseline after 24 hr (Figure 6a).
evidence: Shown in Figure 6a.

claim: Injection of poly(I:C) i.v. into Ifnar-/- mice resulted in a significantly blunted elevation of GZMA.
source: Injection of poly(I:C) i.v. into Ifnar-/- mice resulted in a significantly blunted elevation of GZMA (Figure 6a).
evidence: Shown in Figure 6a with statistical significance (p=0.004).

claim: Type I IFNs appear to augment rapid GZMA release after poly(I:C) injection.
source: Type I IFNs thus appear to augment this rapid GZMA release; however, the absence of type I IFN signaling does not prevent GZMA secretion, consistent with previous data (Schanoski et al., 2019).
evidence: Inferred from the blunted but not absent GZMA elevation in Ifnar-/- mice (Figure 6a) and supported by citation (Schanoski et al., 2019).

claim: The absence of type I IFN signaling does not prevent GZMA secretion.
source: Type I IFNs thus appear to augment this rapid GZMA release; however, the absence of type I IFN signaling does not prevent GZMA secretion, consistent with previous data (Schanoski et al., 2019).
evidence: Shown by GZMA elevation in Ifnar-/- mice after poly(I:C) (Figure 6a) and supported by citation (Schanoski et al., 2019).

claim: Poly(I:C) treatment of GzmaS211A mice resulted in serum GZMA levels not significantly different from those seen in 6J mice.
source: Poly(I:C) treatment of GzmaS211A mice resulted in serum GZMA levels not significantly different from those seen in 6J mice (Figure 6a), illustrating that the active site mutation does not significantly affect production, secretion, or stability.
evidence: Shown in Figure 6a.

claim: The active site mutation in GzmaS211A does not significantly affect GZMA production, secretion, or stability.
source: Poly(I:C) treatment of GzmaS211A mice resulted in serum GZMA levels not significantly different from those seen in 6J mice (Figure 6a), illustrating that the active site mutation does not significantly affect production, secretion, or stability.
evidence: Inferred from comparable serum GZMA levels in GzmaS211A and 6J mice after poly(I:C) treatment (Figure 6a).

claim: No serum GZMB was detected after poly(I:C) treatment.
source: Finally, although GZMB and GZMA are often considered to be co-expressed (Supplementary file 1), in this setting no serum GZMB was detected (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: GZMB and perforin proteins are not expressed in resting NK cells.
source: GZMB and perforin proteins are not expressed in resting NK cells and appear only after ≈24 hr of appropriate stimulation (Fehniger et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation (Fehniger et al., 2007).

claim: GZMB and perforin proteins appear only after approximately 24 hours of appropriate stimulation.
source: GZMB and perforin proteins are not expressed in resting NK cells and appear only after ≈24 hr of appropriate stimulation (Fehniger et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation (Fehniger et al., 2007).

claim: RNA-Seq of GzmaS211A vs 6J feet after poly(I:C) injection identified 199 differentially expressed genes.
source: Of the 199 DEGs identified in the feet of poly(I:C)-treated GzmaS211A vs. 6J mice, 100 were downregulated, with the top annotations associated with negative regulation of protease activity and negative regulation of cell signaling after Cytoscape analysis (Figure 6b, Table 1, Supplementary file 6).
evidence: RNA-Seq data analysis shown in Supplementary file 6b.

claim: 100 DEGs were downregulated in feet of GzmaS211A vs 6J mice after poly(I:C) injection.
source: Of the 199 DEGs identified in the feet of poly(I:C)-treated GzmaS211A vs. 6J mice, 100 were downregulated, with the top annotations associated with negative regulation of protease activity and negative regulation of cell signaling after Cytoscape analysis (Figure 6b, Table 1, Supplementary file 6).
evidence: RNA-Seq data analysis shown in Supplementary file 6b.

claim: The top annotations for downregulated DEGs in GzmaS211A feet were associated with negative regulation of protease activity and negative regulation of cell signaling.
source: Of the 199 DEGs identified in the feet of poly(I:C)-treated GzmaS211A vs. 6J mice, 100 were downregulated, with the top annotations associated with negative regulation of protease activity and negative regulation of cell signaling after Cytoscape analysis (Figure 6b, Table 1, Supplementary file 6).
evidence: Cytoscape analysis shown in Figure 6b, Table 1, and Supplementary file 6e.

claim: GZMA is proteolytically active in vivo.
source: This result supports the view that GZMA is proteolytically active in vivo (Spaeny-Dekking et al., 2000) and that GZMA's proteolytic activity mediates cell signaling events under physiological conditions.
evidence: Supported by citation (Spaeny-Dekking et al., 2000) and RNA-Seq data showing negative regulation of protease activity annotations.

claim: GZMA's proteolytic activity mediates cell signaling events under physiological conditions.
source: This result supports the view that GZMA is proteolytically active in vivo (Spaeny-Dekking et al., 2000) and that GZMA's proteolytic activity mediates cell signaling events under physiological conditions.
evidence: Inferred from RNA-Seq data showing negative regulation of cell signaling annotations in GzmaS211A mice (Table 1).

claim: IPA Disease and Functions analysis identified downregulation of inflammation and leukocyte activation signatures in GzmaS211A feet after poly(I:C).
source: IPA Disease and Functions analysis of the 199 DEGs from feet (GzmaS211A + polyIC vs. 6J + polyIC; Supplementary file 6b) identified downregulation (negative z-scores) of a series of inflammation and leukocyte activation signatures (Figure 6b, Supplementary file 6f).
evidence: IPA analysis shown in Figure 6b and Supplementary file 6f.

claim: STAT6, STAT3, NFATC2, JUN, NFKB1, and STAT1 were the dominant downregulated transcription factor signatures in GzmaS211A mice.
source: An IPA USR analysis using the direct-only interaction option, which largely limits the analysis to transcription factors, showed STAT6, STAT3, NFATC2, JUN, NFKB1, and STAT1 to be the dominant downregulated transcription factor signatures in GzmaS211A mice by z-score and p-values (Figure 6b, Figure 6—figure supplement 4a).
evidence: IPA USR analysis shown in Figure 6b and Figure 6—figure supplement 4a.

claim: STAT3 and NF-κB have been shown to be activated in macrophages by recombinant GZMA in vitro.
source: STAT3 and NF-κB have previously been shown to be activated in macrophages by recombinant GZMA in vitro (Santiago et al., 2020), with monocytes/macrophages reported as targets for GZMA activity in a variety of settings (Garzón-Tituaña et al., 2021; Metkar et al., 2008; Santiago et al., 2017; Spencer et al., 2013; Uranga et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations (Santiago et al., 2020; Garzón-Tituaña et al., 2021; Metkar et al., 2008; Santiago et al., 2017; Spencer et al., 2013; Uranga et al., 2016).

claim: Monocytes/macrophages are reported as targets for GZMA activity in a variety of settings.
source: STAT3 and NF-κB have previously been shown to be activated in macrophages by recombinant GZMA in vitro (Santiago et al., 2020), with monocytes/macrophages reported as targets for GZMA activity in a variety of settings (Garzón-Tituaña et al., 2021; Metkar et al., 2008; Santiago et al., 2017; Spencer et al., 2013; Uranga et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations (Garzón-Tituaña et al., 2021; Metkar et al., 2008; Santiago et al., 2017; Spencer et al., 2013; Uranga et al., 2016).

claim: Gene sets associated with activated monocytes were significantly enriched in the downregulated genes for GzmaS211A + polyIC vs. 6J + polyIC.
source: Interrogation of the Molecular Signature Database (MSigDB) (Subramanian et al., 2005) using GSEAs also identified gene sets associated with activated monocytes (GSE19888) that were significantly enriched in the downregulated genes for GzmaS211A + polyIC vs. 6J + polyIC (Figure 6—figure supplement 4b).
evidence: GSEA analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4b.

claim: Only 4 DEGs were identified in the spleen of poly(I:C)-treated GzmaS211A vs. 6J mice.
source: Circulating proteolytically active GZMA would appear to have limited influence in the spleen as only four DEGs were identified in the spleen of poly(I:C)-treated GzmaS211A vs. 6J mice (Supplementary file 6d).
evidence: RNA-Seq data shown in Supplementary file 6d.

claim: The only significantly upregulated DEG in GzmaS211A spleens was Mid1.
source: Interestingly, the only significantly upregulated DEG in GzmaS211A spleens was Mid1, a gene involved in controlling granule exocytosis by cytotoxic lymphocytes (Boding et al., 2014; Boding et al., 2015).
evidence: RNA-Seq data in Supplementary file 6d and supported by citations (Boding et al., 2014; Boding et al., 2015).

claim: Mid1 is a gene involved in controlling granule exocytosis by cytotoxic lymphocytes.
source: Interestingly, the only significantly upregulated DEG in GzmaS211A spleens was Mid1, a gene involved in controlling granule exocytosis by cytotoxic lymphocytes (Boding et al., 2014; Boding et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations (Boding et al., 2014; Boding et al., 2015).

claim: The activity of GZMA in the periphery is not significantly recapitulated in spleen after poly(I:C) treatment.
source: GSEA also illustrated that neither up- nor downregulated DEGs identified in the feet were enriched in spleen (Figure 6—figure supplement 3), arguing that in this setting the activity of GZMA in the periphery is not significantly recapitulated in spleen.
evidence: GSEA analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: Serum GZMA levels during CHIKV infection and arthritis were substantially lower than those seen after poly(I:C) treatment.
source: Firstly, the serum GZMA levels during CHIKV infection and arthritis (≈0.2 and ≈0.075 ng/ml) were substantially lower than those seen after poly(I:C) treatment (≈20 ng/ml) (Figure 7c), and very much lower than the ≈5 µg of recombinant GZMA-injected intraplantar to generate overt foot swelling in the absence of any other stimuli (Schanoski et al., 2019).
evidence: Shown in Figure 7c and supported by citation (Schanoski et al., 2019).

claim: Only small overlaps were evident between DEGs upregulated during CHIKV infection and DEGs upregulated by proteolytically active GZMA.
source: Secondly, when the DEGs (q < 0.05) that were upregulated in feet during CHIKV peak viremia (day 2) and peak arthritis (day 7 in the Wilson et al. study) (6J + CHIKV vs. 6J mock infection) were compared with DEGs upregulated by proteolytically active GZMA (6J + poly(I:C) vs. GzmaS211A + poly(I:C); Supplementary file 6b), only small overlaps were evident, 27 genes for day 2 and 20 genes for day 7 (Figure 7c, Supplementary file 6i).
evidence: Shown in Figure 7c and Supplementary file 6i.

claim: The magnitude of cytokine USR effects was very much smaller for poly(I:C) treatment compared to CHIKV infection.
source: Thirdly, although CHIKV infection showed upregulation of many transcription factor and cytokine USRs (Supplementary file 2h), with some of these also upregulated by poly(I:C) treatment (Supplementary file 6g), the magnitude of the effects (by p-value and z-scores) was very much smaller for poly(I:C) treatment (shown for cytokine USRs, Figure 7d).
evidence: Shown in Figure 7d comparing cytokine USRs.

claim: GZMA only plays a minor role in stimulating immune and inflammation pathways during CHIKV viremia and arthritis.
source: So CHIKV infection (day 2) and arthritis (day 6) stimulate immune and inflammation pathways that overlap with those stimulated by GZMA, but GZMA only plays a minor role in stimulating these pathways during CHIKV viremia (day 2) and arthritis (day 6).
evidence: Inferred from the small overlap in DEGs and smaller magnitude of effects for GZMA compared to CHIKV.

claim: Gzma-/-/Gzmb-/- double-knockout mice would also very likely have full-length Nnt.
source: The close association of Nnt and Gzma genes also means Gzma-/-Gzmb-/- double-knockout mice (Supplementary file 1) would also very likely have full-length Nnt.
evidence: Inferred from the close genetic linkage of Nnt and Gzma genes on chromosome 13.

claim: Another Gzma-/- mouse generated using 129/SvJ ES cells would likely have the same Nnt issue.
source: Another Gzma-/- mouse generated using 129/SvJ ES cells (Shresta et al., 1997) would likely have the same issue as 129/SvJ mice also have a full-length Nnt gene.
evidence: Inferred from knowledge that 129/SvJ mice have full-length Nnt and supported by citation (Shresta et al., 1997).

claim: 129/SvJ mice have a full-length Nnt gene.
source: Another Gzma-/- mouse generated using 129/SvJ ES cells (Shresta et al., 1997) would likely have the same issue as 129/SvJ mice also have a full-length Nnt gene.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge.

claim: The 6J genome has a 12-nucleotide insertion at the Nnt exon 8–12 deletion junction.
source: Alignment of the WGS of Gzma-/- mice (PRJNA664888) to the standard 6J MM10 mouse genome build allowed identification of the neomycin cassette insertion site into the Gzma gene that was used to generate the Gzma-/- mice (Ebnet et al., 1995; Figure 3a). Curiously, this alignment shows a 12-nucleotide insertion in the 6J genome at the Nnt exon 8–12 deletion junction (Figure 3b).
evidence: Shown in Figure 3b by WGS alignment.

claim: The 12 nucleotides at the Nnt deletion junction are absent in other 6N WGS data.
source: The 12 nucleotides are also absent in other 6N WGS data (Figure 3—figure supplement 3a), indicating this is not a unique feature of Gzma-/- mice.
evidence: Shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3a.

claim: The 12-nucleotide insertion in 6J may have accompanied deletion of Nnt exons 8–12 during the generation of 6J mice.
source: This insertion in 6J may have accompanied deletion of Nnt exons 8–12 during the generation of 6J mice (Fontaine and Davis, 2016; Figure 3—figure supplement 3b).
evidence: Speculated based on WGS data (Figure 3—figure supplement 3b) and supported by citation (Fontaine and Davis, 2016).

claim: Gzmb-/- mice are missing Nnt exons 8–12, consistent with a 6J background.
source: In a separate RT-PCR run, Gzmb-/- mice (Wilson et al., 2017) were shown to be missing Nnt exons 8–12, consistent with a 6J background (Figure 3e).
evidence: Shown by RT-PCR in Figure 3e.

claim: Pronounced foot swelling in all comparisons was associated with upregulation of TNF, IFNG, and IL-6 USRs.
source: Perhaps consistent with the arthritis literature in general (Kato, 2020; Ma and Xu, 2013; Ogata et al., 2019; Suhrbier, 2019), pronounced foot swelling in all comparisons (including MitoTEMPO, see below) was associated with upregulation of TNF, IFNG, and IL-6 USRs (Figure 4e, red box).
evidence: Shown in Figure 4e and supported by citations (Kato, 2020; Ma and Xu, 2013; Ogata et al., 2019; Suhrbier, 2019).

claim: IL-13 was a consistently upregulated USR associated with foot swelling.
source: IL-13 was also a consistently upregulated USR, with IL-13 associated with resolution of arthritic inflammation (Schett, 2019), with peak CHIKV arthritis in 6J mice associated with a significant resolution phase signature (Prow et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations (Schett, 2019; Prow et al., 2019).

claim: IL-13 is associated with resolution of arthritic inflammation.
source: IL-13 was also a consistently upregulated USR, with IL-13 associated with resolution of arthritic inflammation (Schett, 2019), with peak CHIKV arthritis in 6J mice associated with a significant resolution phase signature (Prow et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation (Schett, 2019).

claim: Peak CHIKV arthritis in 6J mice is associated with a significant resolution phase signature.
source: IL-13 was also a consistently upregulated USR, with IL-13 associated with resolution of arthritic inflammation (Schett, 2019), with peak CHIKV arthritis in 6J mice associated with a significant resolution phase signature (Prow et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation (Prow et al., 2019).

claim: MitoTEMPO has been widely used as an experimental antioxidant treatment to scavenge mitochondrial ROS in a variety of disease settings.
source: MitoTEMPO has been widely used as an experimental antioxidant treatment to scavenge mitochondrial ROS in a variety of disease settings (Aoyama et al., 2012; Li et al., 2018; To et al., 2020; Vincent et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations (Aoyama et al., 2012; Li et al., 2018; To et al., 2020; Vincent et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2020).

claim: MitoTEMPO treatment may be correcting the Nnt defect in 6J mice by scavenging excess mitochondrial ROS.
source: However, MitoTEMPO treatment may simply be correcting (at least in part, Figure 4e) the Nnt defect in 6J mice by scavenging excess mitochondrial ROS arising from the loss of functional NNT (Ward et al., 2020).
evidence: Speculated based on the mechanism of MitoTEMPO and NNT function, supported by citation (Ward et al., 2020).

claim: More than 300 papers listed in PubMed use MitoTEMPO in 6J mice.
source: Perhaps noteworthy is that >300 papers listed in PubMed use MitoTEMPO in 6J mice, with many reporting effective disease amelioration with MitoTEMPO treatments, for example (Aoyama et al., 2012; Li et al., 2018; To et al., 2020; Vincent et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2020).
evidence: Based on PubMed literature search and supported by example citations.

claim: Antioxidants have not shown clear benefits in human clinical trials.
source: Unfortunately, antioxidants have not shown clear benefits in human clinical trials (Casas et al., 2020; Jiang et al., 2020; Kovacic, 2020; Steinhubl, 2008).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations (Casas et al., 2020; Jiang et al., 2020; Kovacic, 2020; Steinhubl, 2008).

claim: The Jackson Laboratory generated the 6J inbred mouse strain in the 1920s–1930s.
source: The Jackson Laboratory generated the 6J inbred mouse strain in the 1920s–1930s, with this mouse strain the most frequently used mouse strain in biomedical research.
evidence: Stated as historical fact.

claim: The 6J mouse strain is the most frequently used mouse strain in biomedical research.
source: The Jackson Laboratory generated the 6J inbred mouse strain in the 1920s–1930s, with this mouse strain the most frequently used mouse strain in biomedical research.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge.

claim: Differences in the Nnt gene have previously been reported as underappreciated in metabolism research.
source: Although differences in the Nnt gene (or other background genes) have previously been reported as underappreciated in metabolism research (Fontaine and Davis, 2016), the data herein and elsewhere argue that this issue extends to other areas of research (Bourdi et al., 2011; Leskov et al., 2017; McCambridge et al., 2019; Morales-Hernandez et al., 2018; Rao et al., 2020; Ripoll et al., 2012; Salerno et al., 2019; Vozenilek et al., 2018; Williams et al., 2021; Wolf et al., 2016), with age effects also reported (Ghosh et al., 2014; Ubaida-Mohien et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations (Fontaine and Davis, 2016; Bourdi et al., 2011; Leskov et al., 2017; McCambridge et al., 2019; Morales-Hernandez et al., 2018; Rao et al., 2020; Ripoll et al., 2012; Salerno et al., 2019; Vozenilek et al., 2018; Williams et al., 2021; Wolf et al., 2016; Ghosh et al., 2014; Ubaida-Mohien et al., 2019).

claim: Mouse strain listing errors or inadequate backcrossing to 6J appear to be common for SRA RNA-Seq submissions.
source: Mouse strain listing errors or inadequate backcrossing to 6J would thus appear to be common for SRA RNA-Seq submissions.
evidence: Inferred from the high percentage (27%) of Run Accessions with Nnt reads inconsistent with 6J background.

claim: Nnt has been reported to affect redox regulation and activation in macrophages.
source: However, Nnt has been reported to affect redox regulation and activation in macrophages (Ripoll et al., 2012; Salerno et al., 2019), with an intact Nnt gene conceivably reducing cross-presentation (Dingjan et al., 2016; Nalle et al., 2020) and CD8 T cell responses (Oberkampf et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations (Ripoll et al., 2012; Salerno et al., 2019).

claim: An intact Nnt gene may reduce cross-presentation.
source: However, Nnt has been reported to affect redox regulation and activation in macrophages (Ripoll et al., 2012; Salerno et al., 2019), with an intact Nnt gene conceivably reducing cross-presentation (Dingjan et al., 2016; Nalle et al., 2020) and CD8 T cell responses (Oberkampf et al., 2018).
evidence: Speculated based on citations (Dingjan et al., 2016; Nalle et al., 2020).

claim: An intact Nnt gene may reduce CD8 T cell responses.
source: However, Nnt has been reported to affect redox regulation and activation in macrophages (Ripoll et al., 2012; Salerno et al., 2019), with an intact Nnt gene conceivably reducing cross-presentation (Dingjan et al., 2016; Nalle et al., 2020) and CD8 T cell responses (Oberkampf et al., 2018).
evidence: Speculated based on citation (Oberkampf et al., 2018).

claim: Circulating GZMA in humans is proteolytically active.
source: GZMA's bioactivity has generally (Plasman et al., 2014; Schanoski et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2020), but not always (Shimizu et al., 2019; van Eck et al., 2017), been associated with GZMA's protease activity, with circulating GZMA in humans shown to be proteolytically active (Spaeny-Dekking et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation (Spaeny-Dekking et al., 1998).

claim: Humans, nonhuman primates, and mice have elevated serum GZMA levels after infection with CHIKV.
source: We have shown previously that humans, nonhuman primates, and mice have elevated serum GZMA levels after infection with CHIKV (Schanoski et al., 2019; Wilson et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations (Schanoski et al., 2019; Wilson et al., 2017).

claim: Infection of mice with a series of RNA viruses resulted in high serum GZMA levels early in infection.
source: Infection of mice with a series of other RNA viruses also resulted in high serum GZMA levels early in infection, with NK cells identified as the likely source (Schanoski et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation (Schanoski et al., 2019).

claim: NK cells were identified as the likely source of elevated serum GZMA after RNA virus infection.
source: Infection of mice with a series of other RNA viruses also resulted in high serum GZMA levels early in infection, with NK cells identified as the likely source (Schanoski et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation (Schanoski et al., 2019).

claim: Resting NK cells constitutively contain abundant levels of GZMA protein.
source: Resting NK cells constitutively contain abundant levels of GZMA protein (Fehniger et al., 2007), which is usually stored in granules as a mature protease, with the low pH of the granule preventing (premature) proteolytic activity (Stewart et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations (Fehniger et al., 2007; Stewart et al., 2012).

claim: GZMA is usually stored in granules as a mature protease.
source: Resting NK cells constitutively contain abundant levels of GZMA protein (Fehniger et al., 2007), which is usually stored in granules as a mature protease, with the low pH of the granule preventing (premature) proteolytic activity (Stewart et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation (Stewart et al., 2012).

claim: The low pH of the granule prevents premature proteolytic activity of GZMA.
source: Resting NK cells constitutively contain abundant levels of GZMA protein (Fehniger et al., 2007), which is usually stored in granules as a mature protease, with the low pH of the granule preventing (premature) proteolytic activity (Stewart et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation (Stewart et al., 2012).

claim: Poly(I:C) can often mimic aspects of the innate responses to RNA viruses.
source: Polyinosinic:polycytidylic acid (poly(I:C)) can often mimic aspects of the innate responses to RNA viruses (Prow et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation (Prow et al., 2017).

claim: Poly(I:C) treatment is known to activate NK cells.
source: Although poly(I:C) treatment is known to activate NK cells (Djeu et al., 1979; Fehniger et al., 2007; Miyake et al., 2009; Ngoi et al., 2008), this rapid and prodigious poly(I:C)-induced release of GZMA into the circulation, to the best of our knowledge, has hitherto not been reported.
evidence: Supported by citations (Djeu et al., 1979; Fehniger et al., 2007; Miyake et al., 2009; Ngoi et al., 2008).

claim: Type I interferons are rapidly induced by poly(I:C).
source: Type I interferons (IFNs) are also rapidly induced by poly(I:C) (Dempoya et al., 2012; Santiago-Raber et al., 2003), and NK cells express the type I IFN receptor and can respond to type I IFNs (Madera et al., 2016; Mizutani et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations (Dempoya et al., 2012; Santiago-Raber et al., 2003).

claim: NK cells express the type I IFN receptor and can respond to type I IFNs.
source: Type I interferons (IFNs) are also rapidly induced by poly(I:C) (Dempoya et al., 2012; Santiago-Raber et al., 2003), and NK cells express the type I IFN receptor and can respond to type I IFNs (Madera et al., 2016; Mizutani et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations (Madera et al., 2016; Mizutani et al., 2012).
